cases.title: Asunción Metrobus: Shops Closed Along an Abandoned Bus Corridor
cases.place: Ruta Mariscal Estigarribia, San Lorenzo and Fernando de la Mora, Asunción metropolitan area, Paraguay
cases.point: Mariscal Estigarribia corridor where the Metrobus works ran (approximate)

lenders.name: Inter-American Development Bank (IDB)
lenders.role: US$125 million sovereign-guaranteed loan PR-L1044, approved 29 September 2010 and in force after Paraguay's Congress ratified it on 27 December 2013; one component, worth US$115.9 million, financed the Metrobus bus rapid transit corridor. Disbursements began in July 2014 (MICI compliance review report).

cases.conditions: The loan financed the design and building of the first metropolitan bus rapid transit corridor, from San Lorenzo to downtown Asunción along Avenida Eusebio Ayala and Ruta Mariscal Estigarribia, carried out by the Ministry of Public Works and Communications (MOPC) (MICI).

companies.name: Mota-Engil
companies.role: Construction contractor for the corridor works

cases.community: In May 2016, 11 requesters (10 business owners and one resident) told MICI the works had caused a considerable fall in sales through traffic congestion and lack of customer access, and that Mercado 4 vendors who would have to move had been offered no relocation option (MICI). Última Hora reported in November 2018 that dozens of shops were hit by the works and some closed because of them; ABC Color reported in 2020 that hundreds of shops lost income and many had to close. In October 2018 the frontage traders' association Apctua said the works had left 195 shops closed and more than 1,200 people jobless, with losses of up to 80% (Última Hora). In November 2018 the President signed Decree 567 creating a temporary assistance programme for vulnerable frontage shops; the public works minister said US$1 million would subsidise 300 small traders (Última Hora). In September 2019 traders said only about 300 of more than 500 businesses on the corridor had received the subsidy and that more were closing (ABC Color). In 2024 the traders' lawyer said at least 250 businesses went bankrupt (ABC Color).
cases.killed_note: The traders' lawyer said in 2024 that some people died after going bankrupt (ABC Color); no deaths are documented or counted.
cases.outcome: MICI's compliance review, published in December 2018, found the programme lacked an overall assessment of how works on one section affected others, found links between the harm alleged and non-compliance with the IDB's environment and resettlement policies (OP-703, OP-710), and judged the construction harm a risk that could materialise (MICI). The Comptroller General reported in November 2018 that the MOPC would fine Mota-Engil G. 13,780 million for delays (Última Hora); the company later abandoned the works (ABC Color). In 2020 the ministry demolished the unfinished stations; the stretch built had cost the state about US$21 million (ABC Color). After the IDB removed the Metrobus component, MICI closed the case on 27 May 2021; MICI says the case led the IDB Group to add economic displacement to its safeguards (MICI).

cases.title: Mareña Renovables Wind Farm: Arrests and Police Clashes on the Isthmus
cases.place: Barra de Santa Teresa (San Dionisio del Mar) and Álvaro Obregón (Juchitán), Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Oaxaca, Mexico
cases.point: Álvaro Obregón, the land entrance to Barra de Santa Teresa where the blockade stood (approximate)

lenders.name: Inter-American Development Bank (IDB)
lenders.role: Private-sector loan ME-L1107 of up to 1,060 million Mexican pesos, approved 23 November 2011; disbursements were made on 7 March, 16 April and 15 May 2012, and none after (MICI compliance review report).

lenders.name: Macquarie Group (Australia), through the Macquarie Mexican Infrastructure Fund and Macquarie Asset Finance (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Developed the project with the Mexican group FEMSA; the borrower was Mareña Renovables Capital (MICI).

cases.conditions: The loan was to finance a 396 MW wind project: 132 Vestas turbines (102 at San Dionisio on the Barra de Santa Teresa sandbar and 30 at Santa María del Mar), three substations, a 52 km transmission line to Ixtepec, six docks and access roads. The power was to go to FEMSA companies and the Cuauhtémoc Moctezuma brewery under a self-supply arrangement (MICI).

companies.name: Macquarie Group
companies.role: Developer through its Mexican infrastructure fund and asset finance subsidiary

companies.name: FEMSA (Fomento Económico Mexicano)
companies.role: Co-developer and buyer of the power

cases.community: In December 2012, 232 residents of seven Ikojts (Huave) and Zapotec communities told MICI that opponents of the project in San Dionisio del Mar and San Mateo del Mar had been threatened, cut off from basic services and physically attacked, that mangroves had been destroyed, and that lagoon fishing, their main source of food and income, would be harmed (MICI). MICI's chronology records the occupation of San Dionisio's town hall by communal landholders in January 2012, a petition to the agrarian tribunal to annul the 2004 land-use contract, blockades at Álvaro Obregón from August 2012, a criminal complaint over the assault of a project opponent in September 2012, and nine people arrested during roadblocks and destruction of machinery between 31 October and 2 November 2012 (MICI).
cases.suppression: On the evening of 1 February 2013 seven state police vans arrived at the Álvaro Obregón blockade, the only land route to Barra de Santa Teresa, and police tried to clear it; Código DH, accompanied by Peace Brigades International, reported a confrontation with stones in which some people were injured, and said state police had protected company staff in earlier attempts to enter the area, including on 31 October 2012. Community communiqués reported that police beat residents on 2 February and detained two fishermen, who were visibly beaten and were released at 1 a.m. on 3 February (Kaosenlared, archived by UNAM).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: Mareña informed its lenders on 14 February 2013 that it had closed its Oaxaca offices, and on 28 February decided not to continue the project (MICI). MICI's 2016 compliance review found the IDB failed to ensure timely disclosure and effective consultation, compliance with local law and early identification of social risks; only 5 of 22 required documents were disclosed; and good-faith consultation with Indigenous communities was not ensured. MICI found the threats to opponents were not caused by the Bank's omissions, but said the Bank had no guidance for working amid social conflict. The Board backed the findings and Management reported its action plan complete in August 2018 (MICI).

cases.title: Marsyangdi Corridor Power Line, Lamjung: Wires Strung Under Police Guard
cases.place: Dordi Rural Municipality and Bajhakhet, Lamjung district, Gandaki Province, Nepal
cases.point: Dordi Rural Municipality, Lamjung, where the 2022 arrests took place (approximate)

lenders.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
lenders.role: Loan of EUR 95 million to the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) for the Power System Expansion Project, approved by the EIB Board on 16 September 2014 (EIB-CM initial assessment) and signed on 20 April 2015 (EIB project page); covered by the EU guarantee for EIB loans outside the EU. The complaint concerns Component 2, the 220 kV Marsyangdi Corridor.

cases.conditions: The project finances high-voltage lines and substations in the Kali Gandaki and Marsyangdi corridors, including a double-circuit 220 kV line of about 112 km from Manang through the Annapurna Conservation Area to Khudi, Udipur and Bharatpur, to carry power from hydropower plants on the Marsyangdi river (EIB; Kathmandu Post).
cases.community: The line passes over homes, land, forests and community spaces of Indigenous communities in Lamjung. Landowners under the right of way were offered compensation of 10% of land value (the NEA told the EIB office it could be up to 20% for this project); complainants said this ignored the fall in land value and difficulty mortgaging land (EIB-CM; Kathmandu Post). A community survey by the advisers found only 30% of 123 affected respondents had learned of the project from officials (Kathmandu Post). In April 2021 the EIB office found no satisfactory evidence of engagement with Indigenous peoples, no stakeholder engagement plan, and resettlement plans not finalised for the Udipur–Bharatpur line although tower building, land acquisition and payments were under way (EIB-CM). Its later monitoring found challenges remained on compensation, especially for the right of way (EIB-CM).
cases.suppression: On 27 April 2022 NEA officials with about 30 police installed wire on a tower on the land of Pabitra Thapa, a single mother of four, without her consent; she was beaten when she protested. On 1 May 2022 police arrested four community members, including her and her 17-year-old son; in custody they were made to sign a promise to stop protesting (FPIC & Rights Forum, LAHURNIP and Accountability Counsel). In December 2021 NEA officials with armed police had threatened Bajhakhet villagers who opposed the line (same source). On 24 May 2022 UN human rights experts wrote to Nepal, the NEA and the EIB about the reported beatings and arrests (LAHURNIP).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: The NEA declined the EIB office's offer of mediation in 2019, saying it had followed domestic law (Kathmandu Post). The office's April 2021 conclusions report found non-compliance on consultation, Indigenous peoples and resettlement, and recommended a corrective action plan, expert hires and tying disbursements to progress. By the end of 2024 it judged five of six recommendations implemented but said challenges on the ground remained (EIB-CM).

cases.title: Malicounda Power Plant: Farmland and House Plots Taken
cases.place: Keur Maissa Faye, Malicounda, Mbour department, Thiès region, Senegal

lenders.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
lenders.role: EUR 51 million loan approved 27 November 2018 and signed 29 June 2022 (AfDB article, via AllAfrica); the AfDB was mandated lead arranger of the senior debt (AllAfrica).

lenders.name: Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa (BADEA), West African Development Bank (BOAD) and OPEC Fund for International Development
lenders.role: Co-lenders of senior debt in a financing of about EUR 154–159 million (AllAfrica).

lenders.name: MP Energy (Melec PowerGen, Lebanon) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Majority shareholder with 55%; Africa50 holds 30% and Senelec 15% (BankTrack).

cases.conditions: A 120 MW plant burning heavy fuel oil, designed to switch to Senegalese gas later; commercial operation began in August 2022 (AllAfrica). Bridge financing was arranged by Oragroup (AllAfrica).
cases.community: The project cleared 18 hectares: 13 households lost farmland and 32 households lost a combined 115 housing plots. In total 765 people were affected. Cash compensation was paid before a resettlement plan was drafted, those affected did not receive the census form that lists their losses, the 1,500,000 CFA francs (about US$2,600) offered per 300 m² plot was considered inadequate, and some people had not been paid (BankTrack, drawing on Lumière Synergie pour le Développement). The project's own 2018 impact study summary puts the plant on about 6 ha of an 18 ha site set aside by the Malicounda council on 13 June 2018, describes rain-fed fields around it, and lists loss of land, production and income among the impacts of clearing the site, to be compensated through a resettlement plan then being prepared (ESIA summary). Residents raised a dust complaint in 2021 (AfDB).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: Lumière Synergie pour le Développement filed a complaint with the AfDB's Independent Recourse Mechanism (RQ 2022/01), alleging failures on land acquisition, compensation and consultation and weak Bank monitoring; it was still under IRM handling in the record consulted (Accountability Console). The AfDB says the 2021 dust complaint was resolved through better monitoring and that a social and economic support action plan is being completed (AfDB).

cases.title: Cirebon 1 Coal Plant: Salt Ponds and Shellfish Grounds Lost
cases.place: Kanci and neighbouring coastal villages, Astanajapura, Cirebon regency, West Java, Indonesia
cases.point: Cirebon 1 power plant on Mundu Bay near Kanci (approximate)

lenders.name: Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC)
lenders.role: Signed the loan agreement for the 660 MW Unit 1 in March 2010 together with private banks, for about US$595 million in all; the loans were fully disbursed when villagers objected in 2016 (JBIC examiners' report). JBIC signed a loan for the Cirebon 2 expansion on 18 April 2017 (FoE Japan).

lenders.name: Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, Mizuho, MUFG, ING Group and the Export-Import Bank of Korea
Marubeni (Japan), Korea Midland Power and Samtan (South Korea), through Cirebon Electric Power (foreign investors)
lenders.role: Own 32.5%, 27.5% and 20% of the operator; Indonesia's Indika Energy holds 20% (JBIC examiners' report).

cases.conditions: No policy conditions; the loans financed a coal plant that began operating in July 2012 (JBIC examiners' report). Construction began in 2008 (Eco-Business).

companies.name: Marubeni Corporation
companies.role: Largest shareholder (32.5%) of Cirebon Electric Power

cases.community: WALHI (Friends of the Earth Indonesia) documented about 3,000 farmers and fisherfolk in Kanci and some five neighbouring coastal villages whose livelihoods were disrupted by the plant; a Kanci fisherman and salt farmer said his family income had more than halved and the salt ponds had given way to the power plants (Eco-Business, 2023). In their November 2016 objection to JBIC, villagers said shellfish picking in Kanci Kulon had disappeared, catches of fish, shrimp and rebon had dropped sharply near the jetty and water intake and outlet, some fishers had quit, and salt-makers lost their pans without compensation. JBIC's examiners found the data showed falling catches and wrote it 'cannot be denied that some influence may have been brought', but that the damage and its cause had not been proven (JBIC examiners, 2017). A peer-reviewed study by geographers at Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia and Universitas Padjadjaran, using satellite images from 1999 to 2019 checked against field measurements, found the Cirebon plants caused a significant rise in suspended sediment and sea surface temperature and a fall in chlorophyll-A and salinity in Mundu Bay, which the authors say disturbs marine habitat and makes good catches harder for fishers (Sustinere, 2020).
cases.killed_note: No deaths are tied to the plant in the sources used; Eco-Business cites a separate estimate of 7,100 premature deaths a year from all coal plants in Indonesia, not counted here.
cases.outcome: JBIC's examiners found no non-compliance in JBIC's monitoring and urged direct dialogue (March 2017). On 19 April 2017, the day after JBIC signed its Cirebon 2 loan, the Bandung administrative court revoked the environmental permit for the 1,000 MW expansion after a suit by six villagers (FoE Japan). In November 2022 the operator signed a deal with the Asian Development Bank and Indonesia's investment authority that could retire Cirebon 1 up to 15 years early (Eco-Business).

cases.title: Abidjan Fourth Bridge: Boribana Homes Demolished Under Police Guard
cases.place: Boribana, Attécoubé, and Adjamé village, Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire
cases.point: Boribana, Attécoubé, on the route of the fourth bridge viaduct (approximate)

lenders.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
lenders.role: Financed the Abidjan Urban Transport Project (PTUA), which includes the fourth bridge; residents' complaints were registered by its Independent Recourse Mechanism in 2018 (IRM notice of registration, via Accountability Console). KOACI called the AfDB a key actor in the bridge project.

cases.conditions: The fourth bridge links Yopougon to the Plateau through Attécoubé and Adjamé, crossing the Ébrié lagoon; works began in July 2018 with the Chinese firm CSCEC (Le360/AFP). The project put the cost at 142 billion CFA francs (Fratmat), and the government said about 34 billion CFA francs (€51 million) was set aside to compensate or rehouse residents (Le360/AFP).
cases.community: On 30 November 2019, two bulldozers under heavy police protection demolished all buildings in the viaduct zone at Boribana; 402 people affected by the project there were evicted, and 13,000 people are affected along the whole project (Fratmat). Residents carrying out their belongings told AFP they had received no compensation; one food-stall owner who had arrived in 1986 said he had lost his work and his house (Le360/AFP). On 11 May 2020 four resident owners from a collective that rejected the amounts offered were evicted; the collective said their buildings were demolished while their appeal was still pending (KOACI).
cases.suppression: The Boribana demolitions of 30 November 2019 were carried out under the protection of a large police deployment (Connectionivoirienne; Fratmat; Le360/AFP). Complainants told the IRM that members of Mouvement Colombe Ivoire were harassed and intimidated (IRM notice, via Accountability Console).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: Complaints from Mouvement Colombe Ivoire, Boribana residents and the chief of Adjamé village, registered by the IRM in 2018, alleged flawed lists of eligible people, undisclosed valuations, disputes over resettlement sites and harm to cultural and religious sites in Adjamé (IRM notice). The project said resident owners were rehoused temporarily at state cost while houses were built on 68 ha found in Anyama and Songon, and that four owners who refused to negotiate had their money placed in an escrow account (Fratmat). The project's deputy coordinator said the collective had lost its court case and that its compensation sat in an escrow account (KOACI).

cases.title: Pan Am Generating Plant, La Chorrera: Noise, Fumes and Arrests
cases.place: El Naranjal, El Arado, La Chorrera district, Panamá Oeste, Panama
cases.point: El Arado, La Chorrera, near the Pan Am Generating plant (approximate)

lenders.name: Inter-American Development Bank (IDB)
lenders.role: Financed the construction and operation of the Pan-Am Generating Ltd. thermoelectric plant (Chorrera Power Project); the last disbursement was on 30 January 2002 (MICI).

cases.conditions: The plant began operating in 1999 with 96 MW, burning bunker C fuel oil; in 2014 the company proposed expanding it to 156 MW (La Prensa).
cases.community: Residents have complained since the plant opened of noise, vibration and fumes; a 2021 complaint to MICI from El Naranjal described skin, eye and respiratory illness, mainly in children (MICI). A resident told TVN that night readings at her house in El Naranjal reached 68 decibels; another showed a roof fully rusted less than three years after it was put on (TVN, 2025). A 2015 criminal complaint cited medical tests done in the United States, and in 2018 prosecutors asked for the plant's legal representative to be tried for environmental crimes after chimneys and storage tanks were found built without permits (La Prensa). In March 2025 the environment minister said investigations had confirmed environmental non-compliance, with files open since 2017, and that the plant had kept burning bunker fuel despite an agreed switch to natural gas (Panamá América). A transformer fire at the plant on 15 March 2025 caused a nationwide blackout (La Prensa).
cases.suppression: In 2015 nine members of the Coordinadora Ciudadana de La Chorrera were detained after blocking the delivery of a generator to the plant (La Prensa).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: MICI did not register the 2021 complaint because it came more than 24 months after the last IDB disbursement, a decision it says is not a judgment on the merits (MICI). The electricity regulator fined the company US$10,000 (La Prensa). In April 2025 a National Assembly commission inspected the plant and asked the Health Ministry to study whether it is linked to respiratory illness; the company says it meets environmental rules and that no official evidence ties it to health harm (La Prensa).
